title: London pollution warning after fog and fireworks
text:

 23 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Reuters Dense fog has descended on parts of London in recent days A high air pollution alert for the capital has been issued by the mayor of London after a weekend of dense fog and fireworks, despite actual levels being lower than expected. 
 Forecasters at Imperial College London advised the Mayor, Lord Khan, to trigger the alert for Tuesday after "moderate" pollution levels had been forecast over the weekend of 7-8 November. 
 "On the advice of forecasters at Imperial College London, the GLA issued a high air pollution alert," a spokesperson for the mayor of London said. 
 Londoners have been advised to walk, cycle and use public transport more frequently, drive less and avoid unnecessary burning at home.
 'Slow to clear'
 "Forecasting pollution levels is complex and moderate pollution levels had been forecast for last weekend," the spokesperson added. 
 Direct alerts were sent to schools, councils and care homes from 5 to 8 November.
 The alert is the fourth issued in the capital this year, with the last one made in June during a heatwave. 
 Additional details have been shared with London's GPs and emergency departments, to make sure they have the correct information to help vulnerable patients, the mayor's office said.
 City Hall issues alerts to Londoners, schools, and London boroughs when moderate, high or very high air pollution is forecast.
 High air pollution alerts are also displayed at public locations across London, including all bus stop countdown signs, as well as on the Underground.
 Lingering fog is expected to clear during Tuesday morning, but is expected to give way to cooler and frosty weather later in the week.
 Met Office chief meteorologist Jason Kelly said: "Persistent high pressure has brought light winds and clear skies, allowing fog to form, while weak November sunshine has meant it is fairly slow to clear.
 "We're expecting one more night of dense fog, with a warning in place for some areas. Increasing cloud and wind should then limit further widespread fog from developing."
